newsitem.title: NIGERIA: FEATURE-Poverty a factor in Nigeria's fundamentalism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Poverty a factor in Nigeria's fundamentalism.

text.p: It has been another tough day for Mohammed whose shop is hidden down a twisting alley of Kano's ancient market in northern Nigeria.
"We have nothing here, only poverty. That's why people join in when the Brothers riot," he says.
For the Moslem Brothers, with their home-grown Shi'ite philosophy, the answer to Nigeria's problems is an Iranian style revolution to overthrow the military government and install Islamic Sharia law.
When he was in school Mohammed wanted to be an accountant. Now he's 28, he sells cloth, and not very much of it.
"I must sympathise with them, the Brothers are our friends," he said.
At least seven people died in September in clashes between Shi'ites and police. The Shi'ites say the death toll is much higher, claiming that more than 30 died in separate incidents.

The trigger for the violence was the arrest of charismatic Shi'ite leader Ibrahim Yakub El-Zak-Zaky, 43, on charges of producing inflammatory leaflets, running an illegal radio station and trying to import arms.
"People will protest about anything right now, they don't have enough to eat," Sheikh Gumbi, a prominent Islamic scholar told Reuters in the northern city of Kaduna.
"This is a major crisis, and if it continues it will spread to so many places."
The arid north has always been the poorest part of Africa's most populous nation. Oil money has flowed from the south, but many northerners do not notice the benefit.

"The whole state of the economy, the lack of work, the lack of recreation, the lack of direction has encouraged people to follow El-Zak-Zaky," Bala Usman, history professor at Zaria university told Reuters.
Islam's presence in Nigeria was consolidated during another period of poverty and despair at the start of the early 19th century by jihad revolutionary Usman Dan Fodio.
But Moslems make up only about half of Nigeria's 100 million people, and most of the Moslems are Sunni, not Shi'ite.
It was only in the 1970s that Shi'ite groups, including El-Zak Zaky's surfaced. Since the Iranian revolution in 1979 they have grown more influential.
"Every Friday for the past six months they have fought with other Moslems in the mosques, wanting their preachers to take over," Usman said.
"They record the fighting on video cameras to send to Iran, and justify their funding."
Any kind of instability in the north is an unwelcome prospect for Nigeria's ruling generals.
"If they break the laws of the land we are ready to break their necks," warned Kaduna police commissioner Yakubu Shaibu.
Nigeria has been in political crisis since 1993, when a previous military government annulled elections that would have ended a decade of army rule.
Strikes and riots followed the detention of the presumed winner, millionaire Moslem businessman Moshood Abiola in 1994, but were largely confined to his southwestern homeland.

"We have had enough of religious trouble in the north, unless stern measures are taken from the onset...it could spread like wildfire," said Tanko Yakasai, a northern politician who backs the military's plan to hand over rule to civilians by October 1998.
"Whenever there is no political activity in Nigeria the vacuum can attract anyone. The sooner political parties are out the sooner this will be abandoned," he added.
With El-Zak Zaky jailed and at least 35 other members arrested for their part in the riots, the leadership of the Moslem Brothers has now been driven underground.

"We are just trying to continue with our programme as usual, teaching Islamic philosophy and working to deliver Nigeria from this corrupt system of government," spokesman Mohammed Ciroma said by telephone from Zaria. He has since been arrested.
